To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the administration of a single dose of low‐dose prednison to women at risk for fetal alloimmune thrombocytopeia and immunoglobulin treatment for the newborn, is effective in preventing neonatal alloimmune Thrombocytopenic purpura.
maternal immunoglobulin G administration and prednisone treatment are safe and effective in preventing alloimmune neonatal thrombocytosis.
maternal administration of low‐dose predonine and IgG treatment during pregnancy is safe for both mother and fetus, and may reduce the risk of neonatal alloimmune thombocytopenia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevention of fetal/neonatal alloimmune thromobocytopenia.
the development of a safe, effective and practical treatment for fetal and neonatal alloimmunity, which is a serious and life‐threatening disease.
the development of a novel, non-invasive, and cost-effective method to detect and monitor the progression of fetal alloimmune thrombocytopaenia (FAT).

the treatment of FNAIT is not well established, and that the use of IVIg and/or corticosteroids is still controversial and should be considered on a case‐by‐case basis.
the use of corticosteroids in pregnant women at risk for FNAIT is a promising treatment option, with a good safety profile and a high success rate in preventing the disease.
low‐dose prednison and immunoglobulin g therapy is safe and effective for the prevention and treatment of neonatal alloimmune Thrombocytopenic purpura.

the combination of low‐dose prednison and IVIg is effective in preventing fetal alloimmune thrombocytes in the high‐risk group of pregnant woman.
